/redwood-benchmarks/latency-per-dollar
Alternate: /benchmarks/production-economics

PRIMARY GOAL

1) Download report (PDF)
2) Explore results (interactive tables by model + region)
3) Start building (get API key) / Book a consult (Dedicated/Private)

- Platform/infra leaders comparing hosting options

—
SECTION: WHAT IS “LATENCY PER $”?

Section header
What does “latency per dollar” measure?

Body copy
Latency per $ captures how much latency you get for a given spend under a defined workload. It’s designed to help engineering teams compare the real tradeoff between speed and cost—without focusing on a single number like “cheapest tokens” or “lowest p50.”

Bullets (short)
- Combines measured latency with metered cost under a fixed workload
- Reported per model and per region
- Supported with p50/p95 latency, throughput, and cost per 1M tokens

Inline explainer (keep non-mathy)
If two configurations have similar cost, the one with lower p95 latency will score better. If two configurations have similar latency, the one with lower cost will score better.

Link (inline)
Read the methodology → (anchors to Methodology section and/or appendix page)

—
SECTION: WHAT’S INSIDE THE REPORT

Section header
What you’ll get

3-column cards (copy)
Card 1 — Results tables
Model-by-model, region-by-region benchmark results with latency/$ plus supporting metrics.

Card 2 — Methodology you can reproduce
Workloads, prompt distributions, concurrency settings, warmup policy, caching/batching controls, and rerun/variance rules.

Card 3 — How to interpret results
Guidance for choosing a deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and avoiding benchmarking pitfalls.

Optional “for teams that…” bullets
Great for teams that:
- Need evidence for infra decisions (latency + cost)
- Are migrating models/providers and need apples-to-apples comparisons
- Want predictable performance across regions

SECTION: WHY REDWOOD IS PUBLISHING THIS

Section header
Why we built this benchmark

Body copy (draft)
As open models proliferate, “which model is best?” isn’t the full question. In production, teams need predictable latency, stable costs, and deployment flexibility. Redwood Inference publishes production economics benchmarks to help engineering teams make decisions with transparent methodology—then verify the results against their own workloads.

Optional trust elements
- “Built by Redwood Performance & Evals”
- “Designed for production, not leaderboard gaming”
- “Re-run policy and variance thresholds included”

Reproduce the benchmark (or adapt it to your workload)

Body copy
We include a “how to reproduce” guide and a minimal harness example so you can validate results and tune the benchmark to your traffic shape.

Steps (short)
1) Choose workload (chat/embeddings) and region
2) Match concurrency + context length distribution
3) Run the harness for multiple windows and compare variance
4) Interpret results using p95 + cost (not just a single chart)

—
SECTION: FAQ

FAQ intro
Questions we expect from engineers, SREs, and procurement.

FAQ 1
Q: Is this benchmark “real world”?
A: It’s designed to represent common production patterns (chat + embeddings) using fixed prompt distributions, concurrency settings, and measurement windows. No benchmark matches every workload, so we publish the methodology and variance notes so you can validate fit.

FAQ 2
Q: Does caching/batching affect results?
A: Yes. The report specifies caching and batching policies used during measurement, including warmup handling and any guardrails applied to keep runs consistent. We also highlight scenarios where different policies may change outcomes.

FAQ 3
Q: Are these results comparable across regions?
A: Yes—within the defined harness and region configurations. Each region is measured independently using the same workload definition and rerun policy. Region differences can be caused by fleet composition, network paths, and capacity conditions; we include variance and rerun notes.

FAQ 4
Q: What models are included?
A: A curated set of high-demand and strategically important open models across several families. The exact list and refresh cadence are documented in the report.

FAQ 5
Q: Do you publish raw logs or customer data?
A: No. The benchmark uses Redwood-controlled test traffic. We do not publish customer-identifying traces or per-request logs.

FAQ 6
Q: How do you compute “latency per $”?
A: It’s derived from measured latency metrics and metered cost under a specified workload, then normalized so comparisons are consistent. Full definition, units, and edge cases are in the methodology appendix.

FAQ 7
Q: Can I reproduce this using my own prompts?
A: Yes. We provide guidance and a minimal harness example so you can run a smaller-scale reproduction using your workload characteristics.

FAQ 8
Q: Can I use this for procurement/vendor evaluation?
A: Yes. The report is designed to be shareable internally. For teams needing strict SLAs, dedicated capacity, or data residency controls, we recommend a consult to map requirements to deployment options.

FAQ 9 (Legal/claims safety)
Q: Are you claiming you’re always the fastest or cheapest?
A: No. We present results under defined conditions, include variance notes, and encourage readers to validate against their workloads. Results may change with different settings, models, or infrastructure.
